notes.text: And fear came upon every soul — Of those who did not join with them: whereby persecution was prevented, till it was needful for them.

And sold their possessions — Their lands and houses; and goods - Their movables. And parted them to all as any one had need - To say the Christians did this only till the destruction of Jerusalem, is not true; for many did it long after. Not that there was any positive command for so doing: it needed not; for love constrained them. It was a natural fruit of that love wherewith each member of the community loved every other as his own soul. And if the whole Christian Church had continued in this spirit, this usage must have continued through all ages. To affirm therefore that Christ did not design it should continue, is neither more nor less than to affirm, that Christ did not design this measure of love should continue. I see no proof of this.

Continuing daily — breaking the bread - in the Lord's Supper, as did many Churches for some ages. They partook of their food with gladness and singleness of heart - They carried the same happy and holy temper through all their common actions: eating and working with the same spirit wherewith they prayed and received the Lord's Supper.
The Lord added daily such as were saved — From their sins: from the guilt and power of them.
Lie down — To repose myself at noon, as the manner was in those hot countries. Green - Where there is both delight and plenty of provisions.
Restoreth — Hebrew. He bringeth it back; from its errors and wandering. For - Not for any worth in me, but for the glory of his justice, and faithfulness, and goodness.
Thy rod and thy staff — Two words denoting the same thing, and both designing God's pastoral care over him.

A table — Thou furnishest me with plenty of provisions and comforts. Oil - With aromatic ointments, which were then used at great feasts; thy comforts delight my soul. Runneth over - Thou hast given me a plentiful portions, signified by the cup, given to the guests by the master of the feast. This psalm is generally thought to have been composed by David, upon bringing the ark of God from the house of Obed- edom, into the tabernacle which David had built for it, 2 Sam. vi, 12, 17. Wherein he hath a farther prospect to the temple, which he earnestly desired and intended to build. Moreover because the tabernacle, and temple, and ark, were types of Christ, and of his church and of heaven. David extended his thoughts to them also, or at least the Holy Ghost designed to comprehend them under these typical expressions. He shews God's sovereignty over the world, ver. 1, 2. Who shall receive his blessing, ver. 3-6. An exhortation to receive Christ, ver. 7-10. A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *A psalm of David.* ((CASS.)) The Prophet foretold the return of the people from Babylon. *The Lord ruleth me.* A psalm of mercy, enumerating ten graces, that all may hope in the mercy of God. ((AUG.)) The Church speaks of Christ.

*In a place of pasture.* ((CASS.)) The first grace, a place of pasture, that is, the divine word, which fattens those who meditate upon it. *Upon the water.* The second grace, the water of refreshment.

*My soul.* ((ID.)) The third grace, etc., *as far as* but first he brought me up upon the water of refreshment, first he converted my soul. *He hath led.* ((ID.)) The fourth, in that he led me upon the precepts of charity. *Upon the paths.* ((AUG.)) The narrower commandments and the more perfect counsels; as it were upon paths few just men walk, even as paths are narrower than roads.

*For though I shall walk.* ((CASS.)) The fifth, that in the shadow of death he fears no evils. *Thou art with me.* ((AUG.)) In the heart by faith, that after the shadow of death I may be with thee. *Thy rod.* ((CASS.)) The sixth, correction; or the rod is strictness, which converts vices. The staff is governance, which upholds the faithful.

*Thou hast prepared in my sight.* ((CASS.)) The seventh, the table of the Lord, the blessed banqueting, the fullness of faith, the heavenly food, of which the Apostle: *He that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself. In my sight a table:* even if not that of the wicked. Of this it is said: *But these at the table of the rich man,* that is, of Christ, *know that thou too must prepare the like,* that is, to suffer as he did. *Thou hast anointed:* the eighth, the anointing of the head, namely of Christ, which was dried up by no barrenness of sin, whence the rest of the members rejoice, because from the head the ointment ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, and unto the skirt of his garment. *And my chalice.* The ninth, the chalice, the blood of Christ, which so inebriates that it makes men sober. *Mine,* because I receive it. Or, thine, because thou givest it. The table and the chalice, flesh and blood, although they are one sacrament, yet under diverse species, because both are taken, are here set down separately.
*And mercy.* ((CASS.)) The tenth, mercy following after unto keeping, which goes before unto the conferring of grace.
*And that I may dwell.* ((HIER.)) This is joined to all the things above. As though: thou hast placed, thou hast brought up, thou hast led, etc., and this to the end that I may dwell.

notes.text: For conscience toward God — From a pure desire of pleasing him. Grief - Severe treatment.
Hereunto are ye — Christians. Called - To suffer wrongfully. Leaving you an example - When he went to God. That ye might follow his steps - Of innocence and patience.

In all these instances the example of Christ is peculiarly adapted to the state of servants, who easily slide either into sin or guile, reviling their fellowservants, or threatening them, the natural result of anger without power. He committed himself to him that judgeth righteously — The only solid ground of patience in affliction. Isaiah liii, 4, 6, 7, 9.

22, 23. In all these instances the example of Christ is peculiarly adapted to the state of servants, who easily slide either into sin or guile, reviling their fellowservants, or threatening them, the natural result of anger without power. He committed himself to him that judgeth righteously - The only solid ground of patience in affliction.

Who himself bore our sins — That is, the punishment due to them. In his afflicted, torn, dying body on the tree - The cross, whereon chiefly slaves or servants were wont to suffer. That we being dead to sin - Wholly delivered both from the guilt and power of it: indeed, without an atonement first made for the guilt, we could never have been delivered from the power. Might live to righteousness - Which is one only. The sins we had committed, and he bore, were manifold.
The bishop — The kind observer, inspector, or overseer of your souls.

glossa.text:
*If for conscience towards God.* If, for God who knows a good intention, some patient man is unjustly beaten by his lord, though he serve him well, and endures it, that is, accounts his sorrows light, this is grace, and by this he is made pleasing to God, and this the grace of faith requires.

*Suffering wrongfully.* If you suffer unjustly, you acquire the grace of God. For if you patiently bear the punishments inflicted by your masters, you, I say, sinning by refusing to obey them, and buffeted by those same masters, that is, often corrected by them, that through buffetings you may be led to obey, what grace will you have thereby? Nothing, on this account shall you receive from God.

*For unto this you are called.* He greatly glorifies the condition of servants, whom, well-doing and beaten without fault by cruel and wicked masters, he affirms to be imitators of the Lord's passion.

*Because Christ also. ((BEDA.))* Whereas above he instructed servants specially, now he instructs the whole Church, that he may recall to the memory of masters also what their author endured for their salvation or deliverance.

*But he delivered himself to him that judged him unjustly.* To those judging according to an unjust law, being himself just. Or, he delivered to God the Father those judging unjustly, that is, those who most wickedly condemned him, and pressed for his death, that by undergoing punishments they might be instructed. He touches upon the evangelical parable, where it is said that the good shepherd, leaving ninety-nine sheep in the desert, came to visit the one that had perished.

*And the bishop.* Or the visitor, which is the same thing. For a bishop, that is, an overseer, because *the eyes of the Lord are upon the just, and his ears unto their prayers.* And, *The Orient from on high hath visited us.*

notes.text: He that entereth not by the door — By Christ. He is the only lawful entrance. Into the sheepfold - The Church. He is a thief and a robber - In God's account. Such were all those teachers, to whom our Lord had just been speaking.

To him the door keeper openeth — Christ is considered as the shepherd, ver. 11. As the door in the first and following verses. And as it is not unworthy of Christ to be styled the door, by which both the sheep and the true pastor enter, so neither is it unworthy of God the Father to be styled the door keeper. See Acts xiv, 27; Colossians iv, 3; Rev. iii, 8; Acts xvi, 14. And the sheep hear his voice - The circumstances that follow, exactly agree with the customs of the ancient eastern shepherds. They called their sheep by name, went before them and the sheep followed them. So real Christians hear, listen to, understand, and obey the voice of the shepherd whom Christ hath sent. And he counteth them his own, dearer than any friend or brother: calleth, advises, directs each by name, and leadeth them out, in the paths of righteousness, beside the waters of comfort.

He goeth before them — In all the ways of God, teaching them in every point, by example as well as by precept; and the sheep follow him - They tread in his steps: for they know his voice - Having the witness in themselves that his words are the wisdom and the power of God. Reader, art thou a shepherd of souls? Then answer to God. Is it thus with thee and thy flock?

They will not follow a stranger — One whom Christ hath not sent, who doth not answer the preceding description. Him they will not follow - And who can constrain them to it? But will flee from him - As from the plague. For they know not the voice of strangers - They cannot relish it; it is harsh and grating to them. They find nothing of God therein.
They — The Pharisees, to whom our Lord more immediately spake, as appears from the close of the foregoing chapter.
I am the door — Christ is both the Door and the Shepherd, and all things.

Whosoever are come — Independently of me, assuming any part of my character, pretending, like your elders and rabbis, to a power over the consciences of men, attempting to make laws in the Church, and to teach their own traditions as the way of salvation: all those prophets and expounders of God's word, that enter not by the door of the sheepfold, but run before I have sent them by my Spirit. Our Lord seems in particular to speak of those that had undertaken this office since he began his ministry, are thieves -Stealing temporal profit to themselves, and robbers - Plundering and murdering the sheep.

If any one — As a sheep, enter in by me - Through faith, he shall be safe - From the wolf, and from those murdering shepherds. And shall go in and out - Shall continually attend on the shepherds whom I have sent; and shall find pasture - Food for his soul in all circumstances.
The thief cometh not but to steal, and to kill, and to destroy — That is, nothing else can be the consequence of a shepherd's coming, who does not enter in by me.

glossa.text: *Amen, amen I say to you.* Because the Pharisees boasted that they saw, which they would be able to do if they were Christ's sheep, the Lord sets forth against their arrogance a similitude of his flock, and of the door by which one enters into the sheepfold, showing that neither wisdom, nor the observance of the law, nor a good life avails anything except through him: without him they are nothing in whatever Jew, or Gentile and philosopher, or Pharisee who teach men to live blessedly, or heretic under the name of Christ; nor yet in Christ preaching, but all of them without him snatch away and kill. *By the door.* That is, through me, as he afterwards expounds. This gate is low: he who wishes to enter through it must humble himself, lest, if he stands upright, he strike against the low gate. *A thief.* Because he calls his own what belongs to another, that is, he makes God's sheep his own. A robber, because what he has stolen he kills. But all who hold and teach the truth in Christ the shepherd are one shepherd.

*Is the shepherd of the sheep.* Christ is properly the shepherd according to the office of feeding the sheep, as he himself afterwards expounds, who through himself as the door enters into the sheepfold of the sheep. But because others are sharers with him in the pastoral office, the things which are properly said of him are fitting to them also in their own manner. The door is that by which one enters; Christ therefore, the shepherd, is himself the door, and whoever is a shepherd under him enters through that same door into the hearts of the sheep; because if he preaches something else, the sheep do not hear; if Christ, the sheep of Christ acknowledge this voice.

*To him the porter openeth.* The porter, that is, Christ who opens himself, or Scripture which leads to Christ, or the Holy Spirit who teaches all truth.

*And the sheep,* etc. ((AUG.)) Some are true sheep, because the Lord knoweth, etc., *as far as* this no one who is his own despises, no stranger hears.

*But they understood not.* The predestined sheep for a time do not know themselves, nor do they hear the voice of the shepherd, but at the end they persevere; on the contrary the wolves for a time hear, but at the end they persevere.

*All,* etc. He is a thief who enters by simony or in some other way against Christ, and after he has entered kills by his bad example, and so is openly a robber. Nor is such a one to be called a hireling, therefore when the wolf comes he does not resist, but yields for a wage. If he does not resist the wolf tearing them by violence, he receives this wage, that he is not torn asunder along with the sheep; but afterwards, by living badly, he corrupts the sheep, and having now slipped back into the other party he becomes a thief or a robber, losing the name of hireling.

*If any man.* Here he plainly shows that not only the shepherd but the sheep also enter through the door. *And he shall go in.* Within, by thinking well; he shall go out, outwardly, by working well for the example of others. Or he shall go in into the Church, that here he may live by faith. Whence he says afterwards: *That they may have life.* And he shall go out of this life, that he may live for ever. Whence afterwards, and may have life more abundantly, and going in and going out shall find pastures.
*But to steal,* etc. He would steal, by usurping to himself what is another's; kill, by drawing them back from the faith; destroy, unto eternal damnation.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name.
We know his voice, and we follow.
He leads us to green pastures and still water.
He restores our souls.
Though we walk through the valley of shadow,
we will fear no evil, for he is with us.
Christ is risen!
Christ is risen, alleluia!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Listen — the shepherd is calling, naming his own, and the gate stands open for everyone who knows his voice.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
He leads us down to green pastures and the quiet water, and there, beside it, he restores the tired soul.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
Even through the valley where the shadow falls, his rod and his staff are near, and we are not afraid.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
He spreads a table for us, and goodness and mercy follow us home all the days of our lives.
Christ is risen, alleluia!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The good shepherd calls us each by name.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
He leads us to still water and restores our souls.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
Through the valley of shadow we will not fear.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
He sets a table before us. Come, let us worship.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
